# Comonotone barycentric laws on planar fiber faces

This is the many-input version of the proposed two-endpoint planar
transport selection. It preserves an actual anchored integer-base mean
and produces a bounded-density law on that fiber's face. It does not
assert a parity bound on the number or weights of its inputs.

## 1. A one-dimensional maximality lemma, with a proof

Let gamma_i, i=1,...,k, be finite positive compactly supported measures on
the real line with the SAME mass m>0. Let lambda_i>0 sum to one. Let Q_i
be their increasing quantile functions with parameter u in (0,m), so
(Q_i)_*du=gamma_i. Put

    T(u)=sum_i lambda_i Q_i(u),
    rho_max=T_*du.

For any joint coupling Pi of the gamma_i, put

    rho=(sum_i lambda_i x_i)_*Pi.

Then rho and rho_max have equal mass and first moment, and

    integral phi d rho <= integral phi d rho_max       (1)

for every convex real function phi on the common compact range.

Here is a direct proof. If A is any measurable subset of the coupling
space of mass r, its ith coordinate submeasure is bounded above by gamma_i
and has mass r. The integral of x_i against such a submeasure is at most
the upper r-quantile integral integral_(m-r)^m Q_i(u)du. This last assertion
follows by moving any submeasure mass below a threshold to unused mass above
it; equivalently, for every t,

    integral x d alpha <= tr+integral (x-t)_+ d gamma_i,

and minimizing the right side at an r-tail quantile gives the stated bound.
Threshold atoms can be split; the same argument handles all finite measures.

For the call payoff (sum_i lambda_i x_i-c)_+, take A to be its positive
set and r its mass. Thus

    integral (x-c)_+ d rho
       <= sup_(0<=r<=m) [integral_(m-r)^m T(u)du-cr]
        = integral (x-c)_+ d rho_max.                 (2)

The last equality holds because T is nondecreasing: its positive-above-c
set is an upper interval, up to a level set that has zero payoff. Equal
means and (2) imply (1): every convex function on a compact interval is
an affine function plus an integral of call payoffs against its positive
second-derivative measure, or a uniform limit of convex polygonal functions.
This proves maximality without a smoothness or atom-free assumption.

## 2. Exact density control

Suppose additionally gamma_i<=a_i dt, with finite a_i>0. Their quantiles
satisfy, for 0<u<v<m,

    Q_i(v)-Q_i(u) >= (v-u)/a_i                       (3)

at all quantile continuity points, hence with the appropriate monotone
versions everywhere needed. Indeed gamma_i has no atoms, and its cumulative
distribution can increase by v-u across that interval only if its length
is at least (v-u)/a_i. Gaps in the support only strengthen the inequality.

Consequently

    T(v)-T(u) >= (v-u) sum_i lambda_i/a_i.

The inverse image of any interval of length l therefore has Lebesgue
measure at most l/(sum_i lambda_i/a_i). Interval approximation of Borel
sets proves the measure inequality

    rho_max <= [sum_i lambda_i/a_i]^(-1) dt.          (4)

This is sharp when each gamma_i has constant density a_i on an interval
and the quantiles are affine with their respective slopes. The common
support of rho_max need not be the whole interval containing it.

For actual target branches alpha_i of masses lambda_i m with
alpha_i<=dt, set gamma_i=alpha_i/lambda_i. Then (4) gives

    rho_max <= [sum_i lambda_i^2]^(-1) dt.            (5)

The right side depends on the actual barycentric weights. It is not
automatically an integer parity count.

## 3. Actual anchored convex-fiber geometry

Let K_z be compatible planar convex fibers at actual integer bases, and
fix a continuous unit normal n and unit tangent e perpendicular to n.
Take integer input bases z_i and positive weights lambda_i whose mean

    p=sum_i lambda_i z_i

is a sampled integer base. Assume the support relation is TIGHT:

    h_Kp(n)=sum_i lambda_i h_Kzi(n).                 (6)

Write points on each input face as X_i=h_Kzi(n)n+t_i e. Let gamma_i
be measures of common mass m on their tangent coordinates, and suppose
gamma_i<=a_i times face length. Their comonotone barycentric physical law
is the image of du under

    u -> (p, h_Kp(n)n+T(u)e).

For every tuple of input face points, compatibility puts its weighted
barycenter in K_p, and (6) puts it in the face K_p(n). Thus the displayed
law is supported on the ACTUAL face at the integer base p. Equation (4)
is domination by face length there with the same density constant.

Every convex physical test restricted to (p,K_p(n)) is a convex function
of its tangent coordinate. Hence (1) is the full physical convex-order
comparison for any other barycentric coupling of these same input
marginals, not merely a comparison of first moments. The construction
does not change the lattice labels or use an ambient affine normalization.

For a finite planar normal fan this argument can be applied separately
at every normal with such data and then summed. That statement needs no
measurable choice over a continuum of normals. Extending it to a continuously
varying face family would require the corresponding disintegration and
measurability proof; it is not asserted here.

## 4. Scope for the proof search

This supplies an explicit maximal convex-order law with controlled face
density once the actual input marginals and fixed anchored weights have
been provided. It is distinct from an arbitrary conditional endpoint
pairing, which may concentrate at a face midpoint even for bounded target
densities. Replacing a whole physical martingale additionally requires a
martingale from its old source to the newly dominating law and proper
bookkeeping of unchanged target branches; the three-fiber construction
addresses that separately.

No monotonicity of a halfspace indicator follows from convex order. No
analogous maximal coupling is asserted in tangent dimension greater than
one, and no parity-efficient decomposition of arbitrary barycentric rows
is asserted. These remain substantive extra requirements for a general
OC application.
